holidays.name: Eat a Red Apple Day
holidays.description: Kick off winter with a crisp, juicy red apple. Eat it plain, slice it into a salad, or bake it into something cozy. Any red variety counts, from Gala to Red Delicious.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance. It is listed among the fun holidays on December 1, and its creator is unclear.
holidays.funFact: Apples float in water because about 25% of their volume is air. That is why apple bobbing works.

holidays.name: National Cookie Cutter Day
holidays.description: Dig out the cookie cutters, roll out the dough, and turn the kitchen into a shape factory. The day opens National Cookie Cutter Week, which runs December 1–7. It is a good excuse to start the holiday baking season with stars, trees, and gingerbread people.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance that marks the start of the December baking season. Its exact origin is unclear.
holidays.funFact: Cookie cutters became popular in the U.S. through German immigrants, who brought their Christmas cookie-cutting traditions with them.

holidays.name: Bifocals at the Monitor Liberation Day
holidays.description: This day is for everyone who has tilted their head back to squint through the bottom of their glasses at a screen. It encourages you to get proper computer glasses or an eye exam, so you can stop craning your neck at your monitor.
holidays.origin: The day was created by Thomas and Ruth Roy of Wellcat Holidays, who are known for inventing many offbeat observances.
holidays.funFact: Benjamin Franklin is popularly credited with inventing bifocals in the 18th century, so the 'liberation' has a long history.
